# M E T R O N E W S

## From the Legislative Corner

By Todd Vandervort Regional Legislative Meetings This summer, we undertook a major grassroots campaign in the form of meetings with legislators around the State in their district offices reminding them of our opposition to any proposals that allow the sale of wine in grocery stores. We have continued these statewide meetings this fall in hopes of meeting with legislators from each region of the State before the start of session in January. So far, we have had overwhelming support from legislators who have assured us that they will continue to reject any such proposals that come before them. Thanks goes to the liquor store owners who took time out of their busy schedules to participate in those meetings and to Michael Correra who has tirelessly given of his time

and energy. However, this fight is not over – especially with a looming budget deficit and a gap that needs to be filled. We must keep our message strong and garner as much legislative support as possible. We are also asking legislators to send a letter to Governor Paterson urging him to keep any proposals relating to the sale of wine in grocery stores out of budget negotiations. Last year legislators soundly rejected the Gover-nor’s proposal, and they are poised to reject it again if it is raised in the Governor’s budget. Law Revision Commission Report – Part I and Part II The NYS Law Revision Commission released Part I of its review and examination of the Alcoholic Beverage Control Law and its administration by the State Liquor Authority. On behalf of the Association, we submitted

comments to the Commission focusing on our opposition to any proposals that would allow grocery or drug stores to sell wine, as well as our positions on price posting, channel pricing, liquor stores engaging in “other busi-nesses” and the need for additional funding and staffing at the NYS Liquor Authority. Some of the recommendation that the Law Revision Commission issued include the fol-lowing: To address the backlog of more than 3,000 applications dating back to 2008, vacant posi-tions for licensing examiners should be filled; temporary examiners should be hired; legisla-tion should be enacted permitting the is-suance of temporary retail permits and/or the SLA should extend a BYOB privilege to restaurants awaiting licenses. By Michael Correra, Executive Director As I write this column, the days are getting shorter and we are on the eve of our busiest time of year— a period where we are focused on holiday sales and increasing the bottom line for the fiscal year. The weeks ahead are crucial for all of us—but they are equally crucial for the future of our industry. I ask you to take a few moments to think about all that it is going on and ask yourself “What role do I play in making the future better for our industry?” I am very pleased to report that our 75th Annual Metro Dinner was a great success! The revenue pro-duced by this event supports all of the operations of Metro. With the realization that our industry is

under attack, I think we are seeing for the first time, the industry as a whole rallying together. This was certainly seen at the dinner. This was our finest year to date, with 25 more suppliers attending, a 40% in-crease in ticket sales to suppliers and wholesalers, and 80% more retailers taking part in the dinner. This is a great sign that this organization is being embraced by all facets of this wonderful industry. But this coming together is not enough. Yes, we did win the first round in the fight against wine in the grocery stores—but this issue is far from over. Over the last month, I have visited dozens of New York State Senators and Assembly Members. I always begin our meetings by stating how many package

stores are located in their districts. This statement is always followed by the same question: “How many members does Metro PSA have?” The mes-sage here is loud and clear. To be effective in pro-tecting our industry and getting the support of our elected officials in Albany and at the local level— we must be UNIFIED and as STRONG as possible! There is strength in numbers. This is why I am im- ploring all of you who are reading this newsletter to renew your membership in or join Metro PSA for 2010. ## A Vinifera Revolution Michael Correra

Executive Director Michael Towne

### Dr. Konstantin Frank

Wines and Spirits Brooklyn, NY

### Vinifera Wine Cellars

Dr. Konstantin Frank ignited the “Vinifera Revolution” a movement that forever changed the course of wine growing in the Finger Lakes and the United States. Dr. Frank’s vision, knowledge and determi-nation are credited with elevating the New York wine industry from a state of happy mediocrity to a level that today commands world attention.

A European immigrant, Dr. Frank and his family arrived in the United States in 1951. After a brief stay in New York City, Dr. Frank, a professor of plant sciences who held a Ph.D. in viticulture, moved upstate to take a position at Cornell University’s Geneva Experiment Station.

Dr. Frank believed from his years in the Ukraine that the lack of proper rootstock, not the cold climate, was the reason for the failure of Vitis Vinifera vines in the Finger Lakes region. He continued to promote his beliefs and to seek a sympathetic ear, which he found in Charles Fournier, a French champagne Joseph Viscomi maker and president of nearby Gold Seal Vineyards. Communicating in French, Dr. Frank revealed his Chairman research for growing the delicate European vinifera grape varieties in cold climates. For the first time Cappy’s Warehouse the Northeastern United States could produce European varieties of wines. Wine & Spirits In 1962, merely a decade after arriving in America, Dr. Frank founded Vinifera Wine Cellars. The winery Valley Stream, NY quickly earned a reputation for spectacular Rieslings and its original planting of vines formed the backbone of New York’s world-class wines and champagnes.

Never content to rest on his laurels, Dr. Frank’s son, Willy Frank continued the tradition of excellence and determination. Willy amazed the industry in the late 1980’s by releasing an exquisite sparkling wine made at his very own Chateau Frank. Chateau Frank adheres to the “methode champenoise” using the three classic French Champagne grape varieties successfully creating another first for the Finger Lakes Region of New York – world class sparkling wines.

With the help of his cousin Eric Volz as vineyard manager, Willy’s son, Frederick Frank, took over leadership of the winery in 1993 and expanded production with the introduction of a value brand, Salmon Run, which is in honor of the majestic landlocked Salmon and beautiful Keuka Lake. Fred’s business degree from Cornell University and his study of viticulture and enology in Germany helped prepare him ttake over the family business.

Under Fred’s leadership the winery’s production and amount of medals earned has increased greatly and he looks forward to one day turning over the reins to his son, Kyle Konstantin, who hopes to continue as the fourth generation of Franks at the winery. The winery has earned 61 gold medals in 2009 thus far which is more than it has ever recieved and for the fifth year in a row, Dr. Frank's has been named the “Greatest Wine Producer in the Atlantic Northeast” by the Wine Report 2009, 2008, 2007, 2006 and 2005. Most recently, Wine Enthusiast, the highly esteemed national magazine, nominated Dr. Frank's Vinifera Wine Cellars and Chateau Frank for "American Winery of the Year" for their 10th Annual Wine Star Awards. Dr. Frank's is the only Eastern winery in the category.

Dr. Frank’s Wine Cellars is proud of its international winemaking team with each member bringing in their particular expertise. The talented group includes winemakers from California, Australia, France and Germany. The focus on world-class wines continues with each generation of the family, each member living up to the Frank Family tradition of excellence. g

## About ABL

##### Mario D’Amico

Vice Chairman Baldwin’s Grapes and Grains Baldwin, NY

American Beverage Licensees (ABL) is the premier trade association representing the interests of on- and off-premise beverage alcohol retailers. ABL was formed in 2002 after a merger of the on-premise (tav-erns, nightclubs, bars) and off-premise (package stores, liquor stores) national associations. Now with the consolidation and solidarity of a unified retailing front, we are hard at work improving the lives and John W. Semmeles businesses of our members. Vice Chairman Today, ABL’s nearly 20,000 members responsibly Ginny’s serve and sell adult beverages to 15 million customers Wine & Liquor per week in markets throughout the country. ABL Jefferson Valley, NY membership provides nearly 200,000 jobs nation-wide while contributing over $11 billion to the na-tional economy each year, which is a reflection of hardworking, small business owners who have deep connections with their communities, customers and employees. ABL is a federated association comprised of 36 state and regional affiliate associations. In addition to our affiliates, ABL continues to grow thanks in large part to our industry partnerships and coalitions to which we belong. We stand shoulder to shoulder with groups such as the Distilled Spirits Council of the United States (DISCUS), the Beer Institute, the Na-tional Beer Wholesalers Association (NBWA), and the Wine and Spirits Wholesalers of America (WSWA). We share information about threats to our industry, effective techniques of issue management, and coordinate legislative and grassroots efforts. ABL’s leadership is comprised of a board of directors that is led by ABL’s president, currently David Jabour, proprietor of Twin Liquors of Austin, Texas, governs ABL. President O’Laughlin and an execu-tive committee of officers, all of who are democrati-cally elected by the board, comprise the rest of ABL’s leadership. The officers, along with their fellow board members, whom represent each of ABL’s 36 state or regional affiliates, meet three times each year to con-duct the association’s business and determine the path ABL will take to protect the rights of retailers and act as responsible citizens in the alcohol beverage community. The ABL staff, which is led by ABL Executive Direc-tor Harry Wiles, carries out the boards of directors’ decisions. ABL’s headquarters are located on the out -

skirts of Washington, D.C. in Bethesda, Maryland, affording the ABL staff the opportunity to affect po-litical and legislative matters in the nation’s capital. If asked what the defining characteristic, or “raison d’etre”, is for ABL, two words would ring out from a majority of the ABL membership, and those are “gov-ernment affairs”. ABL’s government affairs program largely sets ABL apart from other retailer groups and the industry publishing groups. ABL takes pride in the fact that it is dedicated to national legislative issues that affect its members and the alcohol beverage in-dustry as a whole. ABL represents licensed beverage retailers in the nation’s capital while other industry commentators and pundits sit on the sidelines and add their two cents, without taking a stand and get-ting into the fray. There are a handful of individual issues that ABL monitors and advocates for or against and can be grouped into two categories; alcohol beverage issues and small business issues. Alcohol beverage issues are the most direct and important to ABL, as they are specific to industry that ABL members work in. However, as ABL is comprised of small business own-ers, small business issues are also at the forefront of ABL’s government affairs efforts. ABL has been very active in the ongoing battle to preserve the integrity of the three-tier system of alco-hol distribution and sales. One of ABL’s biggest vic-tories include the permanent repeal of the Special Occupational Tax (SOT) in August 2005. The repeal of this onerous, Civil War-era tax puts money back in the pockets of retailers by saving them $250 per year for each license they own. ABL has also been re-sponsible for preventing the introduction of federal mandates that would have called for states to adopt a one-size-fits-all approach to tackling drunk driving. ABL maintains an active communications and public relations operation, whether it is addressing its members, its industry colleagues, members or Congress, the news media or the public in general. Through a variety of mediums, ABL gets its message out. ABL has grown its capabilities in the past seven years to the point where it can now activate grassroots efforts, respond to an attack, or launch a campaign of its own in a matter of hours.
